facts.answer: Add 1 to 15 Aurora replicas in any of three AZs; Aurora automatically includes them in failover primary selection.
facts.quote: Simply create 1 to 15 replicas in any of three AZs, and Amazon Aurora will automatically include them in failover primary selection.

cross_check.quote: Each Aurora DB cluster can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas in addition to the primary DB instance.
cross_check.answer: Up to 15 Aurora Replicas in addition to the primary; place them in separate Availability Zones.

facts.answer: No. Encrypting an existing unencrypted Aurora instance is not currently supported; create a new encrypted DB instance and migrate the data.
facts.quote: Encrypting an existing unencrypted Aurora instance is not currently supported.

cross_check.quote: You can't convert an unencrypted DB cluster to an encrypted one.
cross_check.answer: No. You can't convert an unencrypted DB cluster to an encrypted one; restore an unencrypted snapshot to an encrypted cluster instead.

facts.answer: Aurora flips the CNAME to the healthy replica, which is promoted to primary; failover typically completes within 30 seconds.
facts.quote: With replicas, Aurora flips the canonical name record (CNAME) to point at the healthy replica, which is promoted to new primary. Failover typically completes within 30 seconds.

facts.answer: Up to 10 secondary DB clusters, each in a different Region.
facts.quote: An Aurora global database has a primary DB cluster in one Region, and up to 10 secondary DB clusters in different Regions.

cross_check.answer: Up to 10 secondary Regions (the same FAQ page also still says five in its cross-Region answer).

facts.answer: It sets up multiple Aurora DB clusters that span multiple AWS Regions, replicating the primary cluster to secondary clusters for fast recovery from a Regional outage and low-latency reads.
facts.quote: With the Amazon Aurora Global Database feature, you set up multiple Aurora DB clusters that span multiple AWS Regions.

facts.answer: No. Use the managed cross-Region failover to promote a secondary Region, and connect through the Global Database writer endpoint to avoid the need to make application code changes.
facts.quote: You can also use the Aurora Global Database writer endpoint to avoid the need to make application code changes.

cross_check.quote: This endpoint is automatically updated to route requests to the writer instance, eliminating the need to update your application each time you change the writer location in your global cluster.
cross_check.answer: No; the global writer endpoint follows the writer, so the application need not be updated.

facts.answer: Typically under a second (replication over dedicated infrastructure).
facts.quote: After any write operation, Aurora replicates data to the secondary AWS Regions using dedicated infrastructure, with latency typically under a second.

facts.answer: Virtually none, because replicas share the cluster volume; typically tens of milliseconds.
facts.quote: We typically observe lag times in the tens of milliseconds.

cross_check.quote: This lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds after the primary instance has written an update.

facts.answer: The volume is split into 10 GiB segments, each replicated six ways across three Availability Zones.
facts.quote: Amazon Aurora automatically divides your database volume into 10 GiB segments spread across many disks. Each segment is replicated six ways across three Availability Zones (AZs).

facts.answer: Aurora Standard charges per I/O request; Aurora I/O-Optimized includes read and write I/O at no additional charge.
facts.quote: With Aurora Standard, you pay per-request for I/O. With Aurora I/O-Optimized, read and write I/O operations are included at no additional charge.

cross_check.quote: Aurora I/O-Optimized – You pay only for the usage and storage of your DB clusters, with no additional charges for read and write I/O operations.
cross_check.answer: I/O-Optimized: no charge for read and write I/O; Standard: a rate per 1 million I/O requests.

facts.answer: Exactly one primary node plus zero to ten read replica nodes (1 to 11 nodes).
facts.quote: A DAX cluster consists of exactly one primary node, and between zero and ten read replica nodes.

cross_check.quote: A DAX cluster can support up to 11 nodes per cluster (the primary node plus a maximum of 10 read replicas).
cross_check.answer: Up to 11 nodes: one primary plus up to 10 replicas.

facts.answer: 11 nodes: the primary plus at most 10 read replicas.
facts.quote: A DAX cluster can support up to 11 nodes per cluster (the primary node plus a maximum of 10 read replicas).

facts.answer: 5 minutes for each cache (item cache and query cache); a custom parameter group sets other TTLs.
facts.quote: The default TTL for each of these caches is 5 minutes.

facts.answer: Eventually consistent reads with microsecond latency.
facts.quote: DAX provides access to eventually consistent data from DynamoDB tables, with microsecond latency.

facts.answer: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), a fully managed, highly available caching service built for DynamoDB.
facts.quote: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, highly available caching service built for Amazon DynamoDB.

cross_check.quote: For these use cases, DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) delivers fast response times for accessing eventually consistent data.

facts.answer: Up to a 10 times performance improvement, from milliseconds to microseconds, even at millions of requests per second.
facts.quote: DAX delivers up to a 10 times performance improvement—from milliseconds to microseconds—even at millions of requests per second.

facts.answer: Apps that require the fastest possible response time for reads; apps that read a small number of items more frequently than others (hot keys); read-intensive but cost-sensitive apps; apps with repeated reads against a large data set.
facts.quote: Applications that require the fastest possible response time for reads.

facts.answer: Cache invalidation, data population and cluster management; it is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so no application logic change is needed.
facts.quote: DAX does all the heavy lifting required to add in-memory acceleration to your DynamoDB tables, without requiring developers to manage cache invalidation, data population, or cluster management.

cross_check.quote: DAX does all the heavy lifting required to add in-memory acceleration to your DynamoDB tables, without requiring you to manage cache invalidation, data population, or cluster management.
cross_check.answer: Cache invalidation, data population and cluster management.

facts.answer: When the application does not need microsecond read times and has no repeated read activity to offload (also strongly consistent, write-intensive, or few repeated reads).
facts.quote: Applications that do not require microsecond response times for reads, or that do not need to offload repeated read activity from underlying tables.

facts.answer: Apps that need strongly consistent reads, write-intensive apps, apps without many repeated reads (DAX performs best above a 90% cache hit rate), and apps that do not need microsecond reads.
facts.quote: Applications without many repeated reads. DAX performs best when cache hit rates exceed 90%.
